entries.source_text: Cognitive aging is often characterized as a process in which two competing forces determine individual development: a genetically driven senescence process that engenders declines in mental mechanics; and an accumulation of life experience that augments cultural, pragmatic, and knowledge-based competence. The considerable variability in the level and rate of change in complex intellectual activities (e.g., language understanding) is often accounted for in terms of individual differences in abilities associated with these forces. I argue that choice in how effort is allocated may be an essential determinant of cognitive change over the life span--both directly, in the form of attentional engagement, and indirectly, as it sculpts neural substrates that give rise to component abilities.

entries.source_text: With life expectancies extended because of medical and other cultural advances, many individuals spend a quarter to a third of their lives in the period characterized as “old age,” a large proportion of which has great potential for vitality in health and mental activity. However, opportunities for intellectual activity often become restricted later in the life span (Riley & Riley, 2000), as do societal expectations for continued cognitive vitality (Hess, Auman, Colcombe, & Rahhal, 2003). In fact, cognitive aging is often characterized as a multifaceted phenomenon, encompassing both growth and decline (Baltes, 1997): While fluid abilities--“mental mechanics” that depend on speeded encoding and transformation of novel information--normatively show declines as a consequence of a genetically driven senescence process, crystallized abilities that depend on knowledge and acquisition of culture can remain stable or increase well into late life. Declines in fluid abilities are a source of concern to researchers and are often deeply disturbing to aging individuals because they are so readily observable: Difficulties with memory, attentional control, and language understanding can hinder a person from participating in everyday life.

entries.source_text: The question raised in this article is whether individuals have some degree of control over these developmental trajectories. In some ways, as we age, we are put in much the same situation as the fictional wizard Harry Potter when he dons the “sorting hat” that selects the house to which he will be assigned at the wizarding school Hogwarts (Rowling, 1997). It is a hard decision for the sorting hat because Harry has certain characteristics of the noble wizards of the house of Gryffindor and the evil wizards of the house of Slytherin (who are also clever and decisive in difficult situations). Hearing the sorting hat’s murmurings, Harry asks not to be put into Slytherin, but into Gryffindor. The hat tries to convince him otherwise, but Harry insists, and the hat finally agrees. Subsequently, as Harry faces terrible ordeals requiring great courage, this interaction troubles him as he wonders whether he is “truly Gryffindor” or “truly Slytherin.”

entries.source_text: Similarly, as we grow older, we struggle with the “sorting hat” of cultural expectations about aging. When faced with intellectual challenges requiring great courage (e.g., keeping track of names at a party, learning new technology, or deciphering retirement plans), we wonder whether we are truly up to the task. We make (implicit and explicit) choices to seek out and engage cognitively challenging situations in meaningful and mindful ways or else to withdraw from activities--either because we buy into cultural stereotypes of diminished cognitive capacity or because opportunities for meaningful intellectual challenge are less available, or both. We often make this choice in cultural contexts in which intellectual capacity is viewed as a fixed entity that cannot be substantially altered through effort (Molden & Dweck, 2006) and in which older adults very typically do not expect to be able to control cognitive outcomes (Hess et al., 2003). To the extent that we do withdraw from intellectual activity, it is possible that performance deteriorates because task-relevant processes are not implemented, as well as because disuse may exaggerate senescence-related declines in cognitive function (which underpins performance).

entries.source_text: Choosing to engage in intellectual activity may be an important determinant of cognitive optimization in two very different senses. First, assuming that cognitive performance ultimately arises from the execution of cognitive operations that underpin that performance, outcomes will be enhanced if computations are conducted effectively (e.g., allocating effort to organizational and elaborative processing for good memory); we can call this implementation of task-specific processes attentional engagement. In other words, effective allocation of attentional resources is important in any cognitive task just to get the job done. The example of language processing will be used to illustrate this principle (Stine-Morrow, Miller, & Hertzog, 2006). Second, habitually selecting environmental contexts that are intellectually stimulating--or activity engagement--may potentially expand capacity (Kramer, Bherer, Colcombe, Dong, & Greenough, 2004). Thus, I propose that habitual self-regulation of one’s cognitive processing and one’s environmental context may contribute to intellectual vitality in later adulthood, both by augmenting performance and by sculpting the cognitive system that engenders future performance.

entries.source_text: In spite of the fact that verbal ability is a crystallized ability that often shows resilience into old age, memory for spoken and written language often reveals declines with age (Johnson, 2003). In our lab, we have investigated the extent to which these deficits may be rooted in nonoptimal attentional engagement. A visual representation of our Self-Regulated Language Processing (SRLP) model (Stine-Morrow, Miller et al., 2006) is presented in Figure 1. Building on contemporary discourse theory, the SRLP model assumes that language understanding and memory arise from the creation of a multifaceted representation of the text’s lexical expression (surface form), its semantic content (ideas), and a perceptually rich representation of the situation suggested by the ideas. There are a number of component processes at each of these three levels (which we can label, word, textbase, and situation model representations) that are needed to construct this representation. Analysis of how process-relevant text characteristics affect reading times can provide indices of how responsive an individual reader is to these text-processing demands. For example, when controlling for surface features (e.g., word length and frequency), we find that readers allocate extra time to words that introduce new concepts, in order to instantiate their contextualized meanings, and that they allocate extra time at the ends of clauses and sentences, in order to integrate these meanings into ideas (for other examples, see Fig. 1). Individual differences in “allocation policy,” operationalized as the relative change in unit reading times as a function of variation in text characteristics (regression coefficients), provide a way to characterize the quality and extent of attentional engagement in reading.

entries.source_text: A recent study in our lab suggests that exertion of effort may be related to both existing capacity and beliefs that effort will lead to good performance. In this study (Stine-Morrow, Shake, Miles, & Noh, 2006), adults read brief texts with the instruction either to read for accuracy or to read for efficiency. Even though the existence of age-related differences in processing capacity would suggest that older adults would need to allocate disproportionate reading time when accurate recall was required, the actual reading time patterns showed the reverse: It was younger readers whose time allocation was especially responsive to the accuracy goal (see Fig. 2). Interestingly, age differences in responsiveness to the accuracy goal (measured as the proportional difference in time allocation between the efficiency and accuracy conditions) could be accounted for in part by both working-memory capacity and memory self-efficacy (based on a paper-and-pencil assessment of beliefs that one can affect outcomes in memory performance). So, regardless of whether or not older adults were actually able to engage the task demands, age differences in self-efficacy contributed to their reluctance to do so. Unpublished data from our lab show that older readers can be induced to engage in more thorough semantic analysis with specific instruction in conceptual integration.

entries.source_text: Fig. 1. The Self-Regulated Language Processing model (Stine-Morrow, Miller, & Hertzog, 2006). In this model, text understanding depends on the construction of a multifaceted mental representation (dark gray box) of the surface form (words), semantic content or ideas expressed by the text (textbase), and the situation described by the text. Each of these three levels of representation can be constructed more or less completely depending on criteria (reference values) that are influenced by the cognitive and socioemotional goals of the reader (top). At each level, attention to relevant processes is regulated by a negative feedback loop, in which the perceived current representation (i.e., perceived word comprehension, perceived textbase comprehension, perceived situational coherence) is compared (C) to the reference value; when the representation is not “good enough,” the processor at that level demands more resources, until equilibrium is reached (i.e., perceived comprehension satisfies reference value). Allocation of effort to specific processes at each level is operationalized as the relative change in reading time as a function of text variables assumed to engage those processes.

entries.source_text: Some evidence suggests that individuals embedded in contexts providing regular opportunities for intellectual challenge (e.g., demanding work environments that require frequent encounters with ill-defined problems; intellectually stimulating leisure pursuits) fare better along a number of dimensions. They are likely to live longer, be more resistant to psychological manifestations of age-related pathological processes (e.g., Alzheimer’s disease, AD), and score better on measures of cognitive performance. While such findings are consistent with the idea that activity engagement has broad-based effects on vitality, they are fundamentally ambiguous, of course, because it may simply be that individuals with higher levels of inherent vitality are more likely to seek out such experiences and to be able to maintain their participation once they find them. In other words, it is plausible that occupational engagement, leisure activities, and vulnerability to dementia (and their trajectories over time) are all just biobehavioral markers for a genetically driven aging process that (as in most biobehavioral processes) is normally distributed in the population, so that these indicators of vitality simply correlate because they derive from a common cause.

entries.source_text: Other evidence for plasticity of core abilities derives from training studies. Probably the most influential exemplar of such research is the ACTIVE trial (Willis et al., 2006), a randomized clinical trial in which older adults were provided 10 sessions of training in certain cognitive abilities (memory, speed, or reasoning). Relative to a no-contact control group, groups who received training showed effects of training, with retention demonstrated up to 5 years. Training effects were highly specific; for example, effects of speed-of-processing training were specific to speeded tasks and did not transfer to memory or reasoning. entries.source_text: In contrast to studies investigating the correlational effects of engaged lifestyle and education, then, experimental training studies (along with studies of expert performance) suggest that the effects of experience are highly specific to the abilities trained. This is a puzzle. One plausible explanation is that an engaged lifestyle might simply exercise a wider array of abilities, but how that broad-based exercise of components might arise is largely unexplored. While engagement has been operationalized in different ways across studies, fundamentally it entails relatively high levels of challenging activity situated in real-life contexts that require self-direction. entries.source_text: So what is the path to cognitive vitality through the life span? The essence of aging is the dynamic interplay between gains and losses. Losses come “for free”; gains are hard won. The literature on resource allocation suggests that there is considerable variability in the extent to which individuals engage the demands of an everyday cognitive task like reading. At the same time, it appears clear from studies of cognitive plasticity that behavioral effects of experience are extremely narrow, so that the effects of activity engagement on broad-based cognitive vitality likely arise because an engaged lifestyle engenders attentional engagement to develop and maintain skills needed for that lifestyle. Intellectually rich contexts that invite self-regulatory efficacy (an education/engagement model as opposed to a training model) may stimulate vitality by providing opportunities to exercise attentional engagement to skill development in ways that are sufficiently meaningful and emotionally satisfying to be self-perpetuating. Key issues that require empirical examination include conditions (e.g., novelty) that support the development and maintenance of attentional and activity engagement, the way in which these two forms of engagement interact, and psychosocial mechanisms (e.g., self-efficacy, control, mindfulness) through which exposure to novelty and nonroutine challenge might engender engagement. Such evidence will test the Dumbledore hypothesis that cognitive vitality depends on both how we engage the task demands of the activities we select and which abilities we sculpt through such activities. As we age, it may well be that it is our choices that show what we truly are.
